The [Church of the Nativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_the_Nativity "Church of the Nativity"), traditionally thought to be the birthplace of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus "Jesus"), is one of several sites to have been designated as a [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") and World Heritage in Danger in the same year. In 2019 it was removed from the danger list.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-1)

The **List of World Heritage in Danger** is compiled by the [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Education,_Scientific,_and_Cultural_Organization "United Nations Education, Scientific, and Cultural Organization") (UNESCO) through the [World Heritage Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Committee "World Heritage Committee"), in accordance with Article 11.4 of the [World Heritage Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Convention "World Heritage Convention"),[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-2) and was established in 1972 to designate and manage [World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-convention-3) The list includes sites that are under threat and whose conservation requires major interventions and for which "assistance has been requested".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-convention-3) It is intended to raise international awareness of these threats and to encourage counteractive measures against them.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-WHinDanger-4) Threats to a site can be either proven imminent threats or potential dangers to a site.

For natural sites, ascertained dangers include the serious decline in the population of an endangered or other valuable species, as well as the deterioration of a property's natural beauty or scientific value caused by human activities. These activities may include logging, pollution, settlement, mining, agriculture or major public works. For cultural properties, ascertained dangers include the serious deterioration of materials, structure, ornamentation, or architectural coherence, as well as the loss of historical authenticity or cultural significance. Potential dangers for both cultural and natural sites include development projects, armed conflicts, inadequate management systems or changes in the legal protective status of the properties. For cultural sites, gradual changes resulting from geological, [climatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"), or environmental factors may also be potential dangers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-opguidelines-5)

Before a property is inscribed on the List of World Heritage in Danger, its condition is assessed and a potential programme for corrective measures is developed in cooperation with the State Party involved. The final decision about inscription is made by the committee. Financial support from the World Heritage Fund may be allocated by the committee for listed properties. The state of conservation is reviewed yearly, after which the committee may request additional measures, delete the property from the list if the threats have ceased or consider deletion from both the List of World Heritage in Danger and the [World Heritage List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_List "World Heritage List").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-opguidelines-5) Of the three [former UNESCO World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Former_UNESCO_World_Heritage_Sites "Former UNESCO World Heritage Sites"), the [Dresden Elbe Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dresden_Elbe_Valley "Dresden Elbe Valley") and the [Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Maritime_Mercantile_City "Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City") were delisted after placement on the List of World Heritage in Danger while the [Arabian Oryx Sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Oryx_Sanctuary "Arabian Oryx Sanctuary") was directly delisted.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-7) Some sites have been designated as World Heritage Sites and World Heritage in Danger in the same year, such as the [Church of the Nativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_the_Nativity "Church of the Nativity"), traditionally considered to be the birthplace of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus "Jesus").

As of May 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger&action=edit), there are 53 sites (14 natural and 39 cultural) on the List of World Heritage in Danger. Arranged by UNESCO regions, 22 of the listed sites are in the Arab States, 12 in Africa, six in Latin America and the Caribbean, six in Asia and the Pacific, and seven in Europe and North America. The majority of the endangered natural sites (nine) are in Africa.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-9) The list encompasses sites identified as facing threats to their integrity, which may arise from natural disasters, armed conflict, neglect, pollution, unsustainable tourism, or other hazards. Among these sites, the impacts of armed conflict are evident in countries such as Syria, where several sites, including the [Ancient City of Aleppo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_City_of_Aleppo "Ancient City of Aleppo") and the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria, endangered as a result of the [Syrian civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrian_civil_war "Syrian civil war"). In Africa, the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo") has multiple listings due to threats such as military conflict and environmental degradation affecting its national parks.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-10)

## Criticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Criticism")]

In some cases, inclusion on the danger list has sparked conservation efforts and prompted the release of funds, benefitting sites such as the [Galápagos Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gal%C3%A1pagos_Islands "Galápagos Islands") and [Yellowstone National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_National_Park "Yellowstone National Park"), both later removed from the List of World Heritage in Danger. Despite this, the list itself and UNESCO's implementation of it have been subject to criticism.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-chape-p87-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-timothy-p83-12) In particular, States Parties and other stakeholders have questioned the authority of the World Heritage Committee to designate a site as in danger without their consent.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p2-3-13)

Until 1992, when UNESCO set a precedent by placing several sites on the danger list against the wishes of the respective States Parties, such parties would typically submit a programme of corrective measures before a site was listed.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-chape-p86-14) Rather than being used solely for its intended purpose, the List of World Heritage in Danger is perceived by some states as a "blacklist" and, according to [Christina Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christina_Cameron "Christina Cameron"), Professor at the School of Architecture and Canada Research Chair on Built Heritage at the University of Montreal, has been used as a political tool to get the attention of States Parties.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-thorsell-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p0-16)

The [International Union for Conservation of Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature "International Union for Conservation of Nature") (IUCN) has noted that UNESCO has, in a number of cases, referenced the List of World Heritage in Danger without formally inscribing a site, particularly where threats could be easily addressed by the State Party.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p18-19-17) The Union has also argued that the prolonged retention of sites on the danger list is questionable and that other mechanisms for conservation should be sought in such cases.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p19-20-18)

## Previously listed sites

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Previously listed sites")]

[![Image 6: A photograph of a fourteen-pointed, silver star with a hole in the middle all attached to a floor above which is draped a purple cloth](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Nativity_Grotto_Star.jpg/250px-Nativity_Grotto_Star.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nativity_Grotto_Star.jpg)

The [Church of the Nativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_the_Nativity "Church of the Nativity"), traditionally thought to be the birthplace of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus "Jesus"), is one of several sites to have been designated as a [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") and World Heritage in Danger in the same year. In 2019 it was removed from the danger list.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-1)

The **List of World Heritage in Danger** is compiled by the [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Education,_Scientific,_and_Cultural_Organization "United Nations Education, Scientific, and Cultural Organization") (UNESCO) through the [World Heritage Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Committee "World Heritage Committee"), in accordance with Article 11.4 of the [World Heritage Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Convention "World Heritage Convention"),[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-2) and was established in 1972 to designate and manage [World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-convention-3) The list includes sites that are under threat and whose conservation requires major interventions and for which "assistance has been requested".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-convention-3) It is intended to raise international awareness of these threats and to encourage counteractive measures against them.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-WHinDanger-4) Threats to a site can be either proven imminent threats or potential dangers to a site.

For natural sites, ascertained dangers include the serious decline in the population of an endangered or other valuable species, as well as the deterioration of a property's natural beauty or scientific value caused by human activities. These activities may include logging, pollution, settlement, mining, agriculture or major public works. For cultural properties, ascertained dangers include the serious deterioration of materials, structure, ornamentation, or architectural coherence, as well as the loss of historical authenticity or cultural significance. Potential dangers for both cultural and natural sites include development projects, armed conflicts, inadequate management systems or changes in the legal protective status of the properties. For cultural sites, gradual changes resulting from geological, [climatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change "Climate change"), or environmental factors may also be potential dangers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-opguidelines-5)

Before a property is inscribed on the List of World Heritage in Danger, its condition is assessed and a potential programme for corrective measures is developed in cooperation with the State Party involved. The final decision about inscription is made by the committee. Financial support from the World Heritage Fund may be allocated by the committee for listed properties. The state of conservation is reviewed yearly, after which the committee may request additional measures, delete the property from the list if the threats have ceased or consider deletion from both the List of World Heritage in Danger and the [World Heritage List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_List "World Heritage List").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-opguidelines-5) Of the three [former UNESCO World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Former_UNESCO_World_Heritage_Sites "Former UNESCO World Heritage Sites"), the [Dresden Elbe Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dresden_Elbe_Valley "Dresden Elbe Valley") and the [Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Maritime_Mercantile_City "Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City") were delisted after placement on the List of World Heritage in Danger while the [Arabian Oryx Sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Oryx_Sanctuary "Arabian Oryx Sanctuary") was directly delisted.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-7) Some sites have been designated as World Heritage Sites and World Heritage in Danger in the same year, such as the [Church of the Nativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_the_Nativity "Church of the Nativity"), traditionally considered to be the birthplace of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesus "Jesus").

As of May 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger&action=edit), there are 53 sites (14 natural and 39 cultural) on the List of World Heritage in Danger. Arranged by UNESCO regions, 22 of the listed sites are in the Arab States, 12 in Africa, six in Latin America and the Caribbean, six in Asia and the Pacific, and seven in Europe and North America. The majority of the endangered natural sites (nine) are in Africa.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-9) The list encompasses sites identified as facing threats to their integrity, which may arise from natural disasters, armed conflict, neglect, pollution, unsustainable tourism, or other hazards. Among these sites, the impacts of armed conflict are evident in countries such as Syria, where several sites, including the [Ancient City of Aleppo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_City_of_Aleppo "Ancient City of Aleppo") and the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria, endangered as a result of the [Syrian civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrian_civil_war "Syrian civil war"). In Africa, the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo") has multiple listings due to threats such as military conflict and environmental degradation affecting its national parks.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-10)

## Criticism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Criticism")]

In some cases, inclusion on the danger list has sparked conservation efforts and prompted the release of funds, benefitting sites such as the [Galápagos Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gal%C3%A1pagos_Islands "Galápagos Islands") and [Yellowstone National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellowstone_National_Park "Yellowstone National Park"), both later removed from the List of World Heritage in Danger. Despite this, the list itself and UNESCO's implementation of it have been subject to criticism.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-chape-p87-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-timothy-p83-12) In particular, States Parties and other stakeholders have questioned the authority of the World Heritage Committee to designate a site as in danger without their consent.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p2-3-13)

Until 1992, when UNESCO set a precedent by placing several sites on the danger list against the wishes of the respective States Parties, such parties would typically submit a programme of corrective measures before a site was listed.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-chape-p86-14) Rather than being used solely for its intended purpose, the List of World Heritage in Danger is perceived by some states as a "blacklist" and, according to [Christina Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christina_Cameron "Christina Cameron"), Professor at the School of Architecture and Canada Research Chair on Built Heritage at the University of Montreal, has been used as a political tool to get the attention of States Parties.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-thorsell-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p0-16)

The [International Union for Conservation of Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature "International Union for Conservation of Nature") (IUCN) has noted that UNESCO has, in a number of cases, referenced the List of World Heritage in Danger without formally inscribing a site, particularly where threats could be easily addressed by the State Party.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p18-19-17) The Union has also argued that the prolonged retention of sites on the danger list is questionable and that other mechanisms for conservation should be sought in such cases.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p19-20-18)

The [Church of the Nativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Church_of_the_Nativity "Church of the Nativity"), traditionally thought to be the birthplace of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Jesus "Jesus"), is one of several sites to have been designated as a [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") and World Heritage in Danger in the same year. In 2019 it was removed from the danger list.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-1)

The **List of World Heritage in Danger** is compiled by the [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/United_Nations_Education,_Scientific,_and_Cultural_Organization "United Nations Education, Scientific, and Cultural Organization") (UNESCO) through the [World Heritage Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_Committee "World Heritage Committee"), in accordance with Article 11.4 of the [World Heritage Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_Convention "World Heritage Convention"),[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-2) and was established in 1972 to designate and manage [World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-convention-3) The list includes sites that are under threat and whose conservation requires major interventions and for which "assistance has been requested".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-convention-3) It is intended to raise international awareness of these threats and to encourage counteractive measures against them.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-WHinDanger-4) Threats to a site can be either proven imminent threats or potential dangers to a site.

For natural sites, ascertained dangers include the serious decline in the population of an endangered or other valuable species, as well as the deterioration of a property's natural beauty or scientific value caused by human activities. These activities may include logging, pollution, settlement, mining, agriculture or major public works. For cultural properties, ascertained dangers include the serious deterioration of materials, structure, ornamentation, or architectural coherence, as well as the loss of historical authenticity or cultural significance. Potential dangers for both cultural and natural sites include development projects, armed conflicts, inadequate management systems or changes in the legal protective status of the properties. For cultural sites, gradual changes resulting from geological, [climatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Climate_change "Climate change"), or environmental factors may also be potential dangers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-opguidelines-5)

Before a property is inscribed on the List of World Heritage in Danger, its condition is assessed and a potential programme for corrective measures is developed in cooperation with the State Party involved. The final decision about inscription is made by the committee. Financial support from the World Heritage Fund may be allocated by the committee for listed properties. The state of conservation is reviewed yearly, after which the committee may request additional measures, delete the property from the list if the threats have ceased or consider deletion from both the List of World Heritage in Danger and the [World Heritage List](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_List "World Heritage List").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-opguidelines-5) Of the three [former UNESCO World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Former_UNESCO_World_Heritage_Sites "Former UNESCO World Heritage Sites"), the [Dresden Elbe Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Dresden_Elbe_Valley "Dresden Elbe Valley") and the [Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Liverpool_Maritime_Mercantile_City "Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City") were delisted after placement on the List of World Heritage in Danger while the [Arabian Oryx Sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Arabian_Oryx_Sanctuary "Arabian Oryx Sanctuary") was directly delisted.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-7) Some sites have been designated as World Heritage Sites and World Heritage in Danger in the same year, such as the [Church of the Nativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Church_of_the_Nativity "Church of the Nativity"), traditionally considered to be the birthplace of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Jesus "Jesus").

As of May 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger&action=edit), there are 53 sites (14 natural and 39 cultural) on the List of World Heritage in Danger. Arranged by UNESCO regions, 22 of the listed sites are in the Arab States, 12 in Africa, six in Latin America and the Caribbean, six in Asia and the Pacific, and seven in Europe and North America. The majority of the endangered natural sites (nine) are in Africa.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-9) The list encompasses sites identified as facing threats to their integrity, which may arise from natural disasters, armed conflict, neglect, pollution, unsustainable tourism, or other hazards. Among these sites, the impacts of armed conflict are evident in countries such as Syria, where several sites, including the [Ancient City of Aleppo](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Ancient_City_of_Aleppo "Ancient City of Aleppo") and the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria, endangered as a result of the [Syrian civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Syrian_civil_war "Syrian civil war"). In Africa, the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo") has multiple listings due to threats such as military conflict and environmental degradation affecting its national parks.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-10)

## Criticism

In some cases, inclusion on the danger list has sparked conservation efforts and prompted the release of funds, benefitting sites such as the [Galápagos Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Gal%C3%A1pagos_Islands "Galápagos Islands") and [Yellowstone National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Yellowstone_National_Park "Yellowstone National Park"), both later removed from the List of World Heritage in Danger. Despite this, the list itself and UNESCO's implementation of it have been subject to criticism.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-chape-p87-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-timothy-p83-12) In particular, States Parties and other stakeholders have questioned the authority of the World Heritage Committee to designate a site as in danger without their consent.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p2-3-13)

Until 1992, when UNESCO set a precedent by placing several sites on the danger list against the wishes of the respective States Parties, such parties would typically submit a programme of corrective measures before a site was listed.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-chape-p86-14) Rather than being used solely for its intended purpose, the List of World Heritage in Danger is perceived by some states as a "blacklist" and, according to [Christina Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Christina_Cameron "Christina Cameron"), Professor at the School of Architecture and Canada Research Chair on Built Heritage at the University of Montreal, has been used as a political tool to get the attention of States Parties.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-thorsell-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p0-16)

The [International Union for Conservation of Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature "International Union for Conservation of Nature") (IUCN) has noted that UNESCO has, in a number of cases, referenced the List of World Heritage in Danger without formally inscribing a site, particularly where threats could be easily addressed by the State Party.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p18-19-17) The Union has also argued that the prolonged retention of sites on the danger list is questionable and that other mechanisms for conservation should be sought in such cases.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p19-20-18)

## Previously listed sites

A number of sites were previously listed as being in danger, but later removed from the list after improvements in management and conservation. [![Image 2: A photograph of a fourteen-pointed, silver star with a hole in the middle all attached to a floor above which is draped a purple cloth](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Nativity_Grotto_Star.jpg/250px-Nativity_Grotto_Star.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/File:Nativity_Grotto_Star.jpg)

The [Church of the Nativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Church_of_the_Nativity "Church of the Nativity"), traditionally thought to be the birthplace of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Jesus "Jesus"), is one of several sites to have been designated as a [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") and World Heritage in Danger in the same year. In 2019 it was removed from the danger list.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-1)

The **List of World Heritage in Danger** is compiled by the [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/United_Nations_Education,_Scientific,_and_Cultural_Organization "United Nations Education, Scientific, and Cultural Organization") (UNESCO) through the [World Heritage Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_Committee "World Heritage Committee"), in accordance with Article 11.4 of the [World Heritage Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_Convention "World Heritage Convention"),[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-2) and was established in 1972 to designate and manage [World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-convention-3) The list includes sites that are under threat and whose conservation requires major interventions and for which "assistance has been requested".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-convention-3) It is intended to raise international awareness of these threats and to encourage counteractive measures against them.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-WHinDanger-4) Threats to a site can be either proven imminent threats or potential dangers to a site.

For natural sites, ascertained dangers include the serious decline in the population of an endangered or other valuable species, as well as the deterioration of a property's natural beauty or scientific value caused by human activities. These activities may include logging, pollution, settlement, mining, agriculture or major public works. For cultural properties, ascertained dangers include the serious deterioration of materials, structure, ornamentation, or architectural coherence, as well as the loss of historical authenticity or cultural significance. Potential dangers for both cultural and natural sites include development projects, armed conflicts, inadequate management systems or changes in the legal protective status of the properties. For cultural sites, gradual changes resulting from geological, [climatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Climate_change "Climate change"), or environmental factors may also be potential dangers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-opguidelines-5)

Before a property is inscribed on the List of World Heritage in Danger, its condition is assessed and a potential programme for corrective measures is developed in cooperation with the State Party involved. The final decision about inscription is made by the committee. Financial support from the World Heritage Fund may be allocated by the committee for listed properties. The state of conservation is reviewed yearly, after which the committee may request additional measures, delete the property from the list if the threats have ceased or consider deletion from both the List of World Heritage in Danger and the [World Heritage List](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_List "World Heritage List").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-opguidelines-5) Of the three [former UNESCO World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Former_UNESCO_World_Heritage_Sites "Former UNESCO World Heritage Sites"), the [Dresden Elbe Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Dresden_Elbe_Valley "Dresden Elbe Valley") and the [Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Liverpool_Maritime_Mercantile_City "Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City") were delisted after placement on the List of World Heritage in Danger while the [Arabian Oryx Sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Arabian_Oryx_Sanctuary "Arabian Oryx Sanctuary") was directly delisted.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-7) Some sites have been designated as World Heritage Sites and World Heritage in Danger in the same year, such as the [Church of the Nativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Church_of_the_Nativity "Church of the Nativity"), traditionally considered to be the birthplace of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Jesus "Jesus").

As of May 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger&action=edit), there are 53 sites (14 natural and 39 cultural) on the List of World Heritage in Danger. Arranged by UNESCO regions, 22 of the listed sites are in the Arab States, 12 in Africa, six in Latin America and the Caribbean, six in Asia and the Pacific, and seven in Europe and North America. The majority of the endangered natural sites (nine) are in Africa.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-9) The list encompasses sites identified as facing threats to their integrity, which may arise from natural disasters, armed conflict, neglect, pollution, unsustainable tourism, or other hazards. Among these sites, the impacts of armed conflict are evident in countries such as Syria, where several sites, including the [Ancient City of Aleppo](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Ancient_City_of_Aleppo "Ancient City of Aleppo") and the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria, endangered as a result of the [Syrian civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Syrian_civil_war "Syrian civil war"). In Africa, the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo") has multiple listings due to threats such as military conflict and environmental degradation affecting its national parks.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-10)

## Criticism

In some cases, inclusion on the danger list has sparked conservation efforts and prompted the release of funds, benefitting sites such as the [Galápagos Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Gal%C3%A1pagos_Islands "Galápagos Islands") and [Yellowstone National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Yellowstone_National_Park "Yellowstone National Park"), both later removed from the List of World Heritage in Danger. Despite this, the list itself and UNESCO's implementation of it have been subject to criticism.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-chape-p87-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-timothy-p83-12) In particular, States Parties and other stakeholders have questioned the authority of the World Heritage Committee to designate a site as in danger without their consent.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p2-3-13)

Until 1992, when UNESCO set a precedent by placing several sites on the danger list against the wishes of the respective States Parties, such parties would typically submit a programme of corrective measures before a site was listed.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-chape-p86-14) Rather than being used solely for its intended purpose, the List of World Heritage in Danger is perceived by some states as a "blacklist" and, according to [Christina Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Christina_Cameron "Christina Cameron"), Professor at the School of Architecture and Canada Research Chair on Built Heritage at the University of Montreal, has been used as a political tool to get the attention of States Parties.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-thorsell-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p0-16)

The [International Union for Conservation of Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature "International Union for Conservation of Nature") (IUCN) has noted that UNESCO has, in a number of cases, referenced the List of World Heritage in Danger without formally inscribing a site, particularly where threats could be easily addressed by the State Party.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p18-19-17) The Union has also argued that the prolonged retention of sites on the danger list is questionable and that other mechanisms for conservation should be sought in such cases.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p19-20-18)

## Previously listed sites

A number of sites were previously listed as being in danger, but later removed from the list after improvements in management and conservation. URL Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger

Published Time: Wed, 16 Sep 2026 10:53:29 GMT

Markdown Content:
[![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2b/World_Heritage_in_Danger._Map_of_countries.svg/500px-World_Heritage_in_Danger._Map_of_countries.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/File:World_Heritage_in_Danger._Map_of_countries.svg)

Countries with World Heritage Sites in danger. Number of sites indicated by colour:

*   Six or more sites 
*   Five sites 
*   Four sites 
*   Three sites 
*   Two sites 
*   One site 

[![Image 2: A photograph of a fourteen-pointed, silver star with a hole in the middle all attached to a floor above which is draped a purple cloth](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/28/Nativity_Grotto_Star.jpg/250px-Nativity_Grotto_Star.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/File:Nativity_Grotto_Star.jpg)

The [Church of the Nativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Church_of_the_Nativity "Church of the Nativity"), traditionally thought to be the birthplace of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Jesus "Jesus"), is one of several sites to have been designated as a [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") and World Heritage in Danger in the same year. In 2019 it was removed from the danger list.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-1)

The **List of World Heritage in Danger** is compiled by the [United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/United_Nations_Education,_Scientific,_and_Cultural_Organization "United Nations Education, Scientific, and Cultural Organization") (UNESCO) through the [World Heritage Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_Committee "World Heritage Committee"), in accordance with Article 11.4 of the [World Heritage Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_Convention "World Heritage Convention"),[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-2) and was established in 1972 to designate and manage [World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-convention-3) The list includes sites that are under threat and whose conservation requires major interventions and for which "assistance has been requested".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-convention-3) It is intended to raise international awareness of these threats and to encourage counteractive measures against them.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-WHinDanger-4) Threats to a site can be either proven imminent threats or potential dangers to a site.

For natural sites, ascertained dangers include the serious decline in the population of an endangered or other valuable species, as well as the deterioration of a property's natural beauty or scientific value caused by human activities. These activities may include logging, pollution, settlement, mining, agriculture or major public works. For cultural properties, ascertained dangers include the serious deterioration of materials, structure, ornamentation, or architectural coherence, as well as the loss of historical authenticity or cultural significance. Potential dangers for both cultural and natural sites include development projects, armed conflicts, inadequate management systems or changes in the legal protective status of the properties. For cultural sites, gradual changes resulting from geological, [climatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Climate_change "Climate change"), or environmental factors may also be potential dangers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-opguidelines-5)

Before a property is inscribed on the List of World Heritage in Danger, its condition is assessed and a potential programme for corrective measures is developed in cooperation with the State Party involved. The final decision about inscription is made by the committee. Financial support from the World Heritage Fund may be allocated by the committee for listed properties. The state of conservation is reviewed yearly, after which the committee may request additional measures, delete the property from the list if the threats have ceased or consider deletion from both the List of World Heritage in Danger and the [World Heritage List](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/World_Heritage_List "World Heritage List").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-opguidelines-5) Of the three [former UNESCO World Heritage Sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Former_UNESCO_World_Heritage_Sites "Former UNESCO World Heritage Sites"), the [Dresden Elbe Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Dresden_Elbe_Valley "Dresden Elbe Valley") and the [Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Liverpool_Maritime_Mercantile_City "Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City") were delisted after placement on the List of World Heritage in Danger while the [Arabian Oryx Sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Arabian_Oryx_Sanctuary "Arabian Oryx Sanctuary") was directly delisted.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-7) Some sites have been designated as World Heritage Sites and World Heritage in Danger in the same year, such as the [Church of the Nativity](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Church_of_the_Nativity "Church of the Nativity"), traditionally considered to be the birthplace of [Jesus](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Jesus "Jesus").

As of May 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger&action=edit), there are 53 sites (14 natural and 39 cultural) on the List of World Heritage in Danger. Arranged by UNESCO regions, 22 of the listed sites are in the Arab States, 12 in Africa, six in Latin America and the Caribbean, six in Asia and the Pacific, and seven in Europe and North America. The majority of the endangered natural sites (nine) are in Africa.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-9) The list encompasses sites identified as facing threats to their integrity, which may arise from natural disasters, armed conflict, neglect, pollution, unsustainable tourism, or other hazards. Among these sites, the impacts of armed conflict are evident in countries such as Syria, where several sites, including the [Ancient City of Aleppo](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Ancient_City_of_Aleppo "Ancient City of Aleppo") and the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria, endangered as a result of the [Syrian civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Syrian_civil_war "Syrian civil war"). In Africa, the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo") has multiple listings due to threats such as military conflict and environmental degradation affecting its national parks.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-10)

## Criticism

In some cases, inclusion on the danger list has sparked conservation efforts and prompted the release of funds, benefitting sites such as the [Galápagos Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Gal%C3%A1pagos_Islands "Galápagos Islands") and [Yellowstone National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Yellowstone_National_Park "Yellowstone National Park"), both later removed from the List of World Heritage in Danger. Despite this, the list itself and UNESCO's implementation of it have been subject to criticism.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-chape-p87-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-timothy-p83-12) In particular, States Parties and other stakeholders have questioned the authority of the World Heritage Committee to designate a site as in danger without their consent.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p2-3-13)

Until 1992, when UNESCO set a precedent by placing several sites on the danger list against the wishes of the respective States Parties, such parties would typically submit a programme of corrective measures before a site was listed.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-chape-p86-14) Rather than being used solely for its intended purpose, the List of World Heritage in Danger is perceived by some states as a "blacklist" and, according to [Christina Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Christina_Cameron "Christina Cameron"), Professor at the School of Architecture and Canada Research Chair on Built Heritage at the University of Montreal, has been used as a political tool to get the attention of States Parties.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-thorsell-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p0-16)

The [International Union for Conservation of Nature](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature "International Union for Conservation of Nature") (IUCN) has noted that UNESCO has, in a number of cases, referenced the List of World Heritage in Danger without formally inscribing a site, particularly where threats could be easily addressed by the State Party.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p18-19-17) The Union has also argued that the prolonged retention of sites on the danger list is questionable and that other mechanisms for conservation should be sought in such cases.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p19-20-18)

## Previously listed sites

A number of sites were previously listed as being in danger, but later removed from the list after improvements in management and conservation. The [Everglades National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/Everglades_National_Park "Everglades National Park") was listed from 1993 to 2007 and has been again since 2010; the [Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/R%C3%ADo_Pl%C3%A1tano_Biosphere_Reserve "Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve") was listed from 1996 to 2007 and has been again since 2011: both are therefore included in the list of currently listed sites (above).[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-:1-42)[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/api/rest_v1/page/html/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-:2-93)

193 United Nations member states

The [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") comprise 193[sovereign states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_state "Sovereign state") and the world's largest [intergovernmental organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_organization "International organization"). All members have equal representation in the [United Nations General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-5)

The [Charter of the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_of_the_United_Nations "Charter of the United Nations") defines the rules for admission of member states. Membership is open to all states which accept certain terms of the charter and are able to carry them out. New members must be recommended by the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council"). In addition to the member states, the UN also invites non-member states to be [observer states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly_observers "United Nations General Assembly observers") at the UN General Assembly. A member state that has persistently violated the principles of the United Nations Charter can be [expelled from the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expulsion_from_the_United_Nations "Expulsion from the United Nations").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-6)

## Membership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Member_states_of_the_United_Nations&veaction=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Membership ") | [edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Member_states_of_the_United_Nations&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section's source code: Membership ")]

The criteria for admission of new members to the UN are established in [Chapter II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_II_of_the_United_Nations_Charter "Chapter II of the United Nations Charter"), Article 4 of the [UN Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_Charter "UN Charter"):[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-charter_ch2-7)

*   Membership in the United Nations is open to all states which accept the obligations contained in the present Charter and, in the judgment of the Organization, are able and willing to carry out these obligations.
*   The admission of any such state to membership in the United Nations will be effected by a decision of the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the [Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council").

A recommendation for admission from the Security Council requires affirmative votes from at least nine of the council's fifteen members, with none of the five [permanent members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent_members_of_the_United_Nations_Security_Council "Permanent members of the United Nations Security Council") using their [veto power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_veto_power "United Nations Security Council veto power"). The [Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council")'s recommendation must then be approved in the [General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly") by a two-thirds majority vote.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-8)

In principle, only [sovereign states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_state "Sovereign state") can become UN members,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-9) and currently, all UN members are sovereign states. Although five members were not sovereign when they joined the UN, they all subsequently became fully independent between 1946 and 1991.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-10) Because a state can only be admitted to membership in the UN by the approval of the Security Council and the General Assembly,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-12)[a number of states that are considered sovereign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_states_with_limited_recognition "List of states with limited recognition") according to the [Montevideo Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo_Convention "Montevideo Convention") are not members of the UN. This is because the UN does not consider them to possess [sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereignty "Sovereignty"), mainly due to the lack of [international recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_recognition "Diplomatic recognition") or due to opposition from one of the permanent members.

In addition to the member states, the UN also invites non-member states to become [observer states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly_observers "United Nations General Assembly observers") at the [UN General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-13) allowing them to participate and speak in General Assembly meetings, but not vote. Observers are generally intergovernmental organizations and international organizations and entities whose statehood or sovereignty is not precisely defined.

The UN officially came into existence on 24 October 1945, after ratification of the [United Nations Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Charter "United Nations Charter") by the [five permanent members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent_members_of_the_United_Nations_Security_Council "Permanent members of the United Nations Security Council") of the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") (the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"), the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), and the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")) and a majority of the other signatories.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-14) A total of 51 original members (or founding members) joined that year; 50 of them signed the Charter at the [United Nations Conference on International Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Conference_on_International_Organization "United Nations Conference on International Organization") in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") on 26 June 1945, while [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland"), which was not represented at the conference, signed it on 15 October 1945.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-originalmembers-16)

United Nations membership status

A number of the original members were not sovereign when they joined the UN, and only gained full independence later:[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-theworldin1945-17)

*   [Belarus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarus "Belarus") (then the [Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byelorussian_Soviet_Socialist_Republic "Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic")) and [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") (then the [Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_Soviet_Socialist_Republic "Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic")) were both [constituent republics of the Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republics_of_the_Soviet_Union "Republics of the Soviet Union"), until gaining full independence in 1991.
*   [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") (whose territory at that time, before the [Partition of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_India "Partition of India"), also included the present-day territories of [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh") and [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan")) was under [British colonial rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj"), until gaining full independence in 1947.
*   [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"), while _de facto_ sovereign at that time, "only gained full capacity to enter into relations with other states in 1947 when it passed the [Statute of Westminster Adoption Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Westminster_Adoption_Act_1947 "Statute of Westminster Adoption Act 1947"). This occurred 16 years after the British Parliament passed the [Statute of Westminster Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Westminster_1931 "Statute of Westminster 1931") in 1931 that recognised New Zealand's autonomy. If judged by the [Montevideo Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo_Convention "Montevideo Convention") criteria, New Zealand did not achieve full _de jure_ statehood until 1947."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-18) However, the UN considers New Zealand to have been independent in 1945, at the time the UN was formed.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-theworldin1945-17)
*   The [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines") (then the [Philippine Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_the_Philippines "Commonwealth of the Philippines")) was a [commonwealth with the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_(U.S._insular_area) "Commonwealth (U.S. insular area)"), until gaining full independence in 1946.

The [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") comprise 193[sovereign states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_state "Sovereign state") and the world's largest [intergovernmental organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_organization "International organization"). All members have equal representation in the [United Nations General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-5)

The [Charter of the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charter_of_the_United_Nations "Charter of the United Nations") defines the rules for admission of member states. Membership is open to all states which accept certain terms of the charter and are able to carry them out. New members must be recommended by the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council"). In addition to the member states, the UN also invites non-member states to be [observer states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly_observers "United Nations General Assembly observers") at the UN General Assembly. A member state that has persistently violated the principles of the United Nations Charter can be [expelled from the United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expulsion_from_the_United_Nations "Expulsion from the United Nations").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-6)

## Membership

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Member_states_of_the_United_Nations&veaction=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Membership ") | [edit source](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Member_states_of_the_United_Nations&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section's source code: Membership ")]

The criteria for admission of new members to the UN are established in [Chapter II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chapter_II_of_the_United_Nations_Charter "Chapter II of the United Nations Charter"), Article 4 of the [UN Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UN_Charter "UN Charter"):[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-charter_ch2-7)

*   Membership in the United Nations is open to all states which accept the obligations contained in the present Charter and, in the judgment of the Organization, are able and willing to carry out these obligations.
*   The admission of any such state to membership in the United Nations will be effected by a decision of the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the [Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council").

A recommendation for admission from the Security Council requires affirmative votes from at least nine of the council's fifteen members, with none of the five [permanent members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent_members_of_the_United_Nations_Security_Council "Permanent members of the United Nations Security Council") using their [veto power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council_veto_power "United Nations Security Council veto power"). The [Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council")'s recommendation must then be approved in the [General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly") by a two-thirds majority vote.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-8)

In principle, only [sovereign states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_state "Sovereign state") can become UN members,[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-9) and currently, all UN members are sovereign states. Although five members were not sovereign when they joined the UN, they all subsequently became fully independent between 1946 and 1991.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-10) Because a state can only be admitted to membership in the UN by the approval of the Security Council and the General Assembly,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-12)[a number of states that are considered sovereign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_states_with_limited_recognition "List of states with limited recognition") according to the [Montevideo Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo_Convention "Montevideo Convention") are not members of the UN. This is because the UN does not consider them to possess [sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereignty "Sovereignty"), mainly due to the lack of [international recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diplomatic_recognition "Diplomatic recognition") or due to opposition from one of the permanent members.

In addition to the member states, the UN also invites non-member states to become [observer states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly_observers "United Nations General Assembly observers") at the [UN General Assembly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly "United Nations General Assembly"),[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-13) allowing them to participate and speak in General Assembly meetings, but not vote. Observers are generally intergovernmental organizations and international organizations and entities whose statehood or sovereignty is not precisely defined.

The world in 1945, after [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). In light blue, the founding members of the United Nations. In dark blue, protectorates and territories of the founding members.

The UN officially came into existence on 24 October 1945, after ratification of the [United Nations Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Charter "United Nations Charter") by the [five permanent members](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permanent_members_of_the_United_Nations_Security_Council "Permanent members of the United Nations Security Council") of the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") (the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)"), [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"), the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), and the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States")) and a majority of the other signatories.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-14) A total of 51 original members (or founding members) joined that year; 50 of them signed the Charter at the [United Nations Conference on International Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Conference_on_International_Organization "United Nations Conference on International Organization") in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") on 26 June 1945, while [Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poland "Poland"), which was not represented at the conference, signed it on 15 October 1945.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-originalmembers-16)

Among the original members, 49 are either still UN members or had their memberships in the UN continued by a [successor state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Succession_of_states "Succession of states")_(see table below)_; for example, the membership of the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") was continued by the [Russian Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia") after its dissolution _(see the section [Former members: Union of Soviet Socialist Republics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding\_members\_of\_the\_United\_Nations#Soviet\_Union\_(1945%E2%80%931991)))_. The other two original members, [Czechoslovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czechoslovakia "Czechoslovakia") and [Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_Federal_Republic_of_Yugoslavia "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia") (i.e., the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia), had been dissolved and their memberships in the UN not continued from 1992 by any one successor state _(see the sections [Former members: Czechoslovakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding\_members\_of\_the\_United\_Nations#Czechoslovakia\_(1945%E2%80%931992)) and [Former members: Yugoslavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding\_members\_of\_the\_United\_Nations#Yugoslavia\_/\_Serbia\_and\_Montenegro\_(1945%E2%80%932006)))_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-originalmembers-16)

At the time of UN's founding, the [seat of China in the UN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_and_the_United_Nations "China and the United Nations") was held by the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%9349) "Republic of China (1912–49)"), but as a result of [United Nations General Assembly Resolution 2758](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_General_Assembly_Resolution_2758 "United Nations General Assembly Resolution 2758") in 1971, it is now held by the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China")_(see the section [Former members: Republic of China (Taiwan)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding\_members\_of\_the\_United\_Nations#Republic\_of\_China\_(1945%E2%80%931971)))_.

United Nations membership status

A number of the original members were not sovereign when they joined the UN, and only gained full independence later:[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-theworldin1945-17)

*   [Belarus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarus "Belarus") (then the [Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byelorussian_Soviet_Socialist_Republic "Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic")) and [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine") (then the [Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukrainian_Soviet_Socialist_Republic "Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic")) were both [constituent republics of the Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republics_of_the_Soviet_Union "Republics of the Soviet Union"), until gaining full independence in 1991.
*   [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") (whose territory at that time, before the [Partition of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_of_India "Partition of India"), also included the present-day territories of [Bangladesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangladesh "Bangladesh") and [Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan "Pakistan")) was under [British colonial rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj"), until gaining full independence in 1947.
*   [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"), while _de facto_ sovereign at that time, "only gained full capacity to enter into relations with other states in 1947 when it passed the [Statute of Westminster Adoption Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Westminster_Adoption_Act_1947 "Statute of Westminster Adoption Act 1947"). This occurred 16 years after the British Parliament passed the [Statute of Westminster Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statute_of_Westminster_1931 "Statute of Westminster 1931") in 1931 that recognised New Zealand's autonomy. If judged by the [Montevideo Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montevideo_Convention "Montevideo Convention") criteria, New Zealand did not achieve full _de jure_ statehood until 1947."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-18) However, the UN considers New Zealand to have been independent in 1945, at the time the UN was formed.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_members_of_the_United_Nations#cite_note-theworldin1945-17)
*   The [Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines "Philippines") (then the [Philippine Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_of_the_Philippines "Commonwealth of the Philippines")) was a [commonwealth with the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_(U.S._insular_area) "Commonwealth (U.S. insular area)"), until gaining full independence in 1946.
